text:
“Yes, love,” he thought again with perfect clarity, “but not the love that loves for something, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love I experienced for the first time when, dying, I saw my enemy and loved him all the same. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and which needs no object. Even now I experience this blissful feeling. To love one’s neighbors, to love one’s enemies. To love everything—to love God in all His manifestations. One can love a dear person with human love; but only an enemy can be loved with divine love. And that was why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?... Loving with human love, one can pass from love to hatred; but divine love cannot change. Nothing, not death, nothing can destroy it. It is the essence of the soul. And how many people I have hated in my life. And of all people, I have loved and hated no one more than her.” And he vividly pictured Natasha to himself, not as he had pictured her before, with only her charm, which gave him joy; but for the first time he pictured her soul. And he understood her feelings, her sufferings, her shame, her remorse. Now, for the first time, he understood all the cruelty of his refusal, saw the cruelty of his break with her. “If only it were possible for me to see her just once more. Once, looking into those eyes, to say...”

And piti-piti-piti and ti-ti, and piti-piti—boom, the fly struck... And his attention was suddenly transferred to another world, a world of reality and delirium, in which something extraordinary was taking place. In that world, the building still went on rising without collapsing; something still stretched out; the candle with the red circle still burned; the same sphinx-shirt lay by the door; but besides all this, something creaked, a breath of fresh wind blew in, and a new white sphinx, standing upright, appeared before the door. And in the head of that sphinx were the pale face and shining eyes of that very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

“Oh, how oppressive this unceasing delirium is!” Prince Andrei thought, trying to banish that face from his imagination. But the face stood before him with the force of reality, and the face drew nearer. Prince Andrei wanted to return to the former world of pure thought, but he could not, and the delirium drew him into its realm. The soft, whispering voice continued its measured babble; something pressed, something stretched out, and the strange face stood before him.

Prince Andrei gathered all his strength to recover his senses; he moved, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, his eyes grew dim, and, like a man plunged into water, he lost consciousness. When he came to, Natasha, that same living Natasha whom, of all the people in the world, he most wished to love with that new, pure, divine love that had now been revealed to him, was kneeling before him. He understood that this was the living, real Natasha, and was not surprised, but quietly rejoiced. Natasha, on her knees, looked at him in fright but as though transfixed (she could not move), holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and motionless. Only in its lower part did something tremble.

Prince Andrei sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.

“You?” he said. “How happy this is!”

With a quick but careful movement, Natasha moved toward him on her knees and, carefully taking his hand, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.

“Forgive me!” she said in a whisper, raising her head and looking at him. “Forgive me!”

“I love you,” said Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me...”

“What is there to forgive?” asked Prince Andrei.

“Forgive me for what I d-did,” Natasha uttered in a barely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more and more rapidly, barely touching it with her lips.

“I love you more, better than before,” said Prince Andrei, raising her face with his hand so that he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, brimming with happy tears, looked at him timidly, compassionately, and with joyful love. Natasha’s thin, pale face with its swollen lips was more than unattractive; it was frightening. But Prince Andrei did not see that face; he saw the radiant eyes, which were beautiful. Voices were heard behind them.

Pyotr the valet, now fully awake, woke the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything that was happening and, carefully covering his undressed body with a sheet, huddled on the bench.

“What is this?” said the doctor, raising himself from his bed. “Be so good as to leave, madam.”

At that same moment, a girl sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter’s absence, was knocking at the door.

Like a somnambulist awakened in the middle of her sleep, Natasha left the room and, on returning to her own hut, fell sobbing onto her bed.

From that day onward, throughout the rest of the Rostovs’ journey, at every halt and overnight stop, Natasha did not leave the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected either such fortitude or such skill in tending a wounded man from a young lady.

However dreadful the thought seemed to the countess that Prince Andrei might—very probably, according to the doctor—die on the journey in her daughter’s arms, she could not oppose Natasha. Although, as a result of the closeness now established between the wounded Prince Andrei and Natasha, it occurred to them that, in the event of his recovery, their former relationship as betrothed man and woman would be renewed, no one, and least of all Natasha and Prince Andrei, spoke of it: the unresolved, looming question of life or death, not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, obscured all other suppositions.

XXXIII.

Pierre awoke late on September 3. His head ached; the clothes in which he had slept without undressing weighed upon his body, and in his soul was a vague awareness of something shameful committed the day before; that shameful thing was yesterday’s conversation with Captain Ramballe.

The clock showed eleven, but outside it seemed particularly overcast. Pierre got up, rubbed his eyes, and, seeing the pistol with the carved stock that Gerasim had put back on the writing desk, Pierre remembered where he was and what lay before him on that very day.

“Can I already be too late?” thought Pierre. “No, he will probably make his entry into Moscow no earlier than twelve.” Pierre did not allow himself to reflect on what lay before him, but hurried to act as soon as possible.

Having straightened his clothes, Pierre took the pistol in his hands and was already preparing to leave. But then, for the first time, the thought occurred to him of how he was to carry this weapon—not openly in his hand—through the streets. Even under his broad caftan, it was difficult to conceal the large pistol. It could not be placed inconspicuously either behind his belt or under his arm. Besides, the pistol was unloaded, and Pierre had not had time to load it. “The dagger will do just as well,” Pierre told himself, though, when discussing the execution of his intention, he had more than once concluded that the chief mistake of the student in 1809 had been that he had wanted to kill Napoleon with a dagger. But as though Pierre’s chief aim were not to carry out his intended deed, but to prove to himself that he was not renouncing his intention and was doing everything to carry it out, Pierre hurriedly took the blunt, notched dagger in a green sheath that he had bought by the Sukharev Tower together with the pistol, and concealed it under his waistcoat.
